extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent agents, and patent examiners in Canada (particularly biotechnology/sequence-related filings)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patentability, sufficiency, claim drafting and sequence-listing requirements under the Canadian Patent Act and Patent Rules, with emphasis on nucleic acids, proteins and sequence listings. Useful for preparing and prosecuting biotechnology-related patent applications in Canada.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem–solution / essential elements analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential elements of a claim are those elements that provide the solution to the identified problem (e.g., data acquisition vs data analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the problem the inventors set out to address in light of the specification and the common general knowledge (CGK) of the POSITA. Elements that provide means to acquire or implement the solution to that identified problem are essential elements of the claim. Elements that solve a different identified problem (e.g., data analysis) may be non-essential for a particular claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory subject-matter (section 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must define subject-matter that falls within a category of invention as defined in section 2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When construing claims, ensure the essential elements put the claim within an allowable category of invention under section 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (subsection 28.2(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is novel if no single prior art document discloses the essential elements of the construed claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the construed essential elements to a single prior art reference. A commercially known plurality-measuring device that does not specifically acquire only the claimed subset of data does not anticipate. Note that change of claim wording (e.g., 'comprising' vs 'consisting') can affect novelty (e.g., 'consisting solely of' may be novel where 'comprising' is not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (section 28.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is non-obvious if the difference between the inventive concept and the prior art would not have been obvious to the POSITA in light of their CGK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the inventive concept, compare to prior art, and determine whether the distinguishing features would have been an obvious step to POSITA. Mere focusing on or disregarding existing data (e.g., disregarding other genes on an array) may or may not be an inventive step depending on whether it represents an obvious step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of the description (subsection 27(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must 'correctly and fully describe the invention and its operation or use as contemplated by the inventor' and must be enabling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description must be clear, accurate, free from avoidable obscurity, and sufficiently full so nothing not described may be validly claimed. It must enable a POSITA to practise the full scope of the claimed invention without inventive effort. If practicing the full scope requires inventive ingenuity, the description is insufficient and claims are unsupported. The description should enable answers to 'What is your invention?: How does it work?'. An objection under subsection 27(3) may be raised where a broad claim is supported only by its own verbatim language or where the description fails to support prediction of utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defect for unsupported claim breadth (relation to section 60 / subsection 27(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define more than the description supports may be defective under section 60 of the Patent Rules and/or subsection 27(3) of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims are broader than the specific examples or embodiments in the description (e.g., a single polypeptide described but claims covering many variants), examiners may identify defects; claim scope must be supported by the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defect for lack of clarity/distinctness (subsection 27(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be defined in distinct and explicit terms; use of variable symbols or vague terms can render a claim non-compliant with subsection 27(4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When structure is needed to realize full scope, claims must include sufficient structural definition. Functional-only definitions may be unacceptable if they lack structural support or lead to unclear scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining biomolecules by structure (sequence identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: For biomolecules, the clearest way to define a molecule is by its structure (e.g., nucleotide or amino acid sequence) and claim should explicitly refer to a SEQ ID NO that points to the sequence listing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to 'SEQ ID NO:x' alone may be interpreted as claims to mere information and be non-compliant with section 2; prefer claims like 'DNA encoding the protein comprising amino acids 1-260 of SEQ ID NO:2'. Beware of variable symbols (X, n) in sequences: they may make the claimed subject-matter indistinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim limitations for biomolecules
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional language can be used to define biomolecules where it provides useful distinction, but the entire scope must be clear and fully supported by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional language is acceptable if POSITA would not need inventive ingenuity to practise the full scope and representative embodiments are disclosed. If functional language requires inventive effort to realise the scope or makes the claim overly broad, the claim may be defective under section 60 of the Rules and/or subsection 27(4). When structure is needed to realise scope, the claim should include structural limitations in addition to function (e.g., percent identity plus statement of same biological activity). Example: where only one polypeptide sequence with xylanase activity is disclosed, broad functional claims or broad percent-identity claims without functional limitation may be defective or anticipated by prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague similarity/homology terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'substantially identical', 'homology', or 'similarity' are inadequate without clear definition and can render a claim indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explicit percent identity thresholds (e.g., 'at least 95% identical to SEQ ID NO:7') and use 'identity' rather than 'homology'. If terms like 'similarity' are used, provide a clear definition of what is meant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims defined by hybridization
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define nucleic acids by hybridization to a target must sufficiently define the hybridization conditions and parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because hybridization/wash conditions affect which nucleic acids are captured, claims relying on hybridization should specify parameters to avoid indefiniteness. If the target is a large family (degenerate sequences), scope can become unclear. If claim implies that a hybridizing nucleic acid encodes a functional polypeptide, the claim may be defective under subsection 27(4) unless the relationship is clear; indicate whether hybridization is to the complement where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence alignment percent identity clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sequence is identified as having a certain percent identity to a reference, it must be stated whether percent identity is relative to the full length of the reference or a partial alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For clarity, full-length alignment is greatly preferred when making percent-identity comparisons (e.g., avoid ambiguous BLAST-style partial alignments unless expressly defined).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness considerations for sequence-based claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an amino acid sequence in the prior art, nucleic acids encoding it are often obvious because they can be deduced by back-translation; conversely a known nucleic acid makes the amino acid sequence obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad claims to 'a nucleic acid encoding protein X' may be obvious where the protein sequence is known. However, selection of a particular nucleic acid species with unexpected/advantageous properties can be inventive and should be analyzed as selection-type claims. Analyze claims against the four-step approach for obviousness, considering whether particular sequence selection would have been obvious to POSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence listing requirement (subsection 58 / PCT ST.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification discloses a nucleotide or amino acid sequence (other than prior art), the description must contain a sequence listing in electronic form that complies with the PCT sequence listing standard (ST.26).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence listings may be English and/or French and must comply with ST.26. If defective, examiners may issue notices under section 65 requiring corrected listings within three months. Missing sequence listings for regularly filed applications may trigger notices under subsection 72(1). Once an electronic ST.26-compliant sequence listing is of record, paper copies of the same listing are not permissible; applicants will be requisitioned to withdraw paper copies. Do not request sequence listings from other applications to satisfy subsection 58(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT ST.26 structure and required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: An XML sequence listing per ST.26 must have a general information part and a sequence data part; each sequence data element must include length, molecule type (DNA/RNA/AA), whether related to a patent application, a feature table, and the sequence itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow ST.26 element requirements (e.g., INSDSeq_length, INSDSeq_moltype, INSDSeq_division, INSDSeq_feature-table, INSDSeq_sequence). Tools such as WIPO Sequence can help prepare compliant listings. See ST.26 Annex III for a complete example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and numbering of sequences in sequence listing
rubrics_metrics.description: Every non-prior-art nucleotide/amino acid sequence disclosed must be included in the sequence listing and assigned a unique sequence identification number starting at 1 and increasing sequentially. Intentionally skipped sequences must use '000'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain original sequence identification numbers even after amendment; when a sequence is removed, replace it with '000' and delete any references to that SEQ ID NO in the specification. The total number of sequences must be indicated (SequenceTotalQuantity) and equal the count of sequence IDs including '000' placeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of sequences used outside the sequence listing (SEQ ID NO references)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sequence included in the sequence listing is referred to in the claims, drawings or other parts of the description, the reference must include the sequence identification number preceded by 'SEQ ID NO:'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to identify sequences by their SEQ ID NO when referenced can be a defect under subsection 58(4). Example: specify both the sequence and '(SEQ ID NO:x)' when listing primers or oligonucleotides in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity symbols and special situations in sequence listings
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity symbols 'n' (nucleotide) and 'X' (amino acid) may be used to represent unknown/variant/modified residues but represent only a single residue at a specific position and have default meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default values: 'n' = any of a,c,g,t/u; 'X' = one of the 20 standard amino acids listed. If used to mean something other than the default value, annotate the symbol in the feature table. For modified nucleotides, when possible represent them as the corresponding unmodified letters. For variable-length sequences, use sufficient discrete symbols to represent the maximum length. Follow ST.26 and accompanying guidance on ambiguous symbols and annotations.
